name: Common cold
simple_definition: A mild, contagious viral infection affecting the nose and upper throat.
medical_definition: An acute, self-limiting viral upper respiratory tract infection, most frequently caused by rhinoviruses.
general_prevention: Avoiding touching face with unwashed hands
common_diagnostic_tests: Clinical assessment based on signs and symptoms
general_treatment: Rest
Adequate hydration
Over-the-counter saline nasal sprays and supportive care as advised by a doctor
when_to_seek_doctor: Consult a healthcare provider if symptoms last more than 10-14 days or worsen significantly.

faqs.q: Do antibiotics cure the common cold?
faqs.a: No. The common cold is caused by viruses, and antibiotics only treat bacterial infections.

source: World Health Organization (WHO) & CDC Guidelines

name: Influenza
simple_definition: A common contagious respiratory illness caused by flu viruses that can cause sudden fever, chills, and body aches.
medical_definition: An acute viral infection of the respiratory tract caused by influenza viruses A, B, or C, characterized by systemic and respiratory symptoms.
general_treatment: Rest, fluids, and clinical evaluation for prescription antiviral medications if initiated early
warning_signs: Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath
when_to_seek_doctor: Prompt medical attention is advised for high-risk individuals or anyone experiencing respiratory distress.

faqs.q: How is influenza different from a common cold?
faqs.a: Flu symptoms typically arrive abruptly and are more severe, notably high fever and profound body ache.

source: CDC Flu Division / WHO Global Influenza Programme

name: Dengue
simple_definition: A mosquito-borne viral infection causing high fever, severe headache, behind-the-eye pain, and severe joint pain.
medical_definition: An acute arboviral illness transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, caused by the dengue virus (DENV 1-4).
possible_causes: Dengue virus transmission via Aedes aegypti / albopictus mosquito bite
risk_factors: Residence or travel in tropical and subtropical endemic regions
Prior infection with another dengue serotype
general_prevention: Eliminating standing water where mosquitoes breed
common_diagnostic_tests: Complete Blood Count (CBC - Platelet count monitoring)
general_treatment: Close medical supervision
Careful oral rehydration
Monitoring platelet count
Avoiding NSAIDs like aspirin/ibuprofen due to bleeding risk
when_to_seek_doctor: Immediate emergency medical attention is essential if warning signs or bleeding occur.

faqs.q: Why is platelet count monitored in dengue?
faqs.a: Dengue can cause transient suppression of bone marrow and destruction of platelets, increasing bleeding risks.

source: World Health Organization (WHO) Dengue Guidelines

name: Malaria
simple_definition: A serious, mosquito-borne parasitic disease characterized by periodic cycles of shaking chills, high fever, and sweating.
medical_definition: A protozoan parasitic infection transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes, caused by Plasmodium species (P. falciparum, P. vivax, etc.).
possible_causes: Plasmodium parasite transmitted by Anopheles mosquito bite
risk_factors: Travel or residence in malaria-endemic areas
Lack of mosquito nets or prophylaxis
common_diagnostic_tests: Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) for malaria antigens
general_treatment: Prescription antimalarial therapy (e.g. Artemisinin-based combination therapies) under medical care
when_to_seek_doctor: Seek emergency medical care immediately upon suspecting malaria to prevent severe complications.

faqs.q: Is malaria preventable?
faqs.a: Yes, through vector control, bed nets, and medically prescribed chemoprophylaxis.

source: World Health Organization (WHO) Malaria Programme

name: Typhoid
simple_definition: A bacterial infection spread through contaminated food and water, causing prolonged step-ladder fever and stomach pain.
medical_definition: An enteric systemic infectious disease caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi.
possible_causes: Salmonella Typhi ingestion from contaminated water or food
general_treatment: Appropriate prescription antibiotics determined by antimicrobial susceptibility testing, with fluids and rest
warning_signs: High persistent fever unresponsive to initial care
when_to_seek_doctor: Medical consultation is required for timely antibiotic treatment and complication prevention.

faqs.q: How does typhoid spread?
faqs.a: Through the fecal-oral route via contaminated food, raw vegetables, or unsafe drinking water.

source: CDC Typhoid Fever Resources

name: COVID-19
simple_definition: A respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus that can range from mild cold-like symptoms to lung inflammation.
medical_definition: An infectious disease caused by the novel severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2).
possible_causes: SARS-CoV-2 viral transmission via respiratory droplets and aerosols
risk_factors: Underlying medical conditions (cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic lung disease)
general_treatment: Supportive hydration, rest, clinical monitoring, and prescription antiviral therapies for high-risk patients
when_to_seek_doctor: Seek emergency medical care immediately for low oxygen saturation, severe shortness of breath, or confusion.

faqs.q: What is the significance of pulse oximetry in COVID-19?
faqs.a: It non-invasively monitors oxygen saturation (SpO2) to detect early respiratory compromise.

source: World Health Organization (WHO) COVID-19 Technical Guidance

name: Migraine
simple_definition: A neurological condition causing intense, pulsating headache attacks, often on one side of the head, with nausea and sensitivity to light.
medical_definition: A primary neurological headache disorder characterized by recurrent attacks of moderate to severe pulsating, unilateral head pain.
possible_causes: Complex neurovascular alterations and trigeminovascular activation
common_diagnostic_tests: Clinical evaluation by a neurologist or physician (imaging if atypical or red-flag features exist)
general_treatment: Acute abortive therapies (e.g. triptans, specific analgesics) prescribed by a doctor; resting in a dark, quiet room
warning_signs: Headache with fever and neck stiffness
Headache with motor weakness or speech difficulty
when_to_seek_doctor: Immediate emergency care is required for sudden, explosive headaches or associated focal neurological deficits.

faqs.q: What is an aura in migraine?
faqs.a: A temporary neurological symptom, usually visual (flashing lights, zigzag patterns) preceding the headache.

source: American Migraine Foundation & National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS)

name: Asthma
simple_definition: A chronic condition where airways narrow, swell, and produce extra mucus, making breathing difficult.
medical_definition: A chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by variable and recurring symptoms, reversible airflow obstruction, and bronchospasm.
possible_causes: Airway hyperresponsiveness triggered by allergens, cold air, exercise, or respiratory infections
risk_factors: Exposure to environmental tobacco smoke or air pollution
general_prevention: Avoiding known triggers (dust mites, pollen, smoke)
general_treatment: Inhaled corticosteroids (controller) and short-acting bronchodilators (rescue) under formal medical management
warning_signs: Severe breathlessness speaking only in single words
when_to_seek_doctor: Severe acute asthma exacerbations require immediate emergency medical care.

faqs.q: Can asthma be cured?
faqs.a: While asthma is chronic, it can be effectively controlled with appropriate medical treatment and action plans.

source: Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) Guidelines

name: Pneumonia
simple_definition: An infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs, which may fill with fluid or pus.
medical_definition: An acute lower respiratory infection causing inflammation of the lung parenchyma, typically involving the alveoli.
common_symptoms: Cough with green, yellow, or bloody mucus
Sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breathing
general_treatment: Physician-prescribed targeted antibiotics or supportive viral therapies, oxygen therapy if indicated, and hydration
when_to_seek_doctor: Pneumonia warrants prompt medical evaluation; respiratory distress requires emergency care.

faqs.q: Is pneumonia contagious?
faqs.a: The underlying causative viruses or bacteria can spread from person to person through respiratory droplets.

source: American Thoracic Society (ATS) / Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA)

name: Diabetes
simple_definition: A chronic metabolic condition characterized by high levels of sugar (glucose) in the bloodstream.
medical_definition: A group of metabolic disorders characterized by persistent hyperglycemia resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both.
possible_causes: Insulin resistance with progressive secretory defect (Type 2)
general_treatment: Lifestyle modification, dietary planning, physician-prescribed oral hypoglycemic agents or insulin
when_to_seek_doctor: Routine ongoing physician management is required; immediate emergency care for symptoms of ketoacidosis or severe hypoglycemia.

faqs.q: What does an HbA1c test show?
faqs.a: It reflects the average blood glucose level over the preceding 2 to 3 months.

source: American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care

name: Hypertension
simple_definition: A condition in which the force of the blood against artery walls is consistently too high (high blood pressure).
medical_definition: A chronic medical condition in which the systemic arterial blood pressure is persistently elevated (systolic >= 130 mmHg and/or diastolic >= 80 mmHg).
possible_causes: Secondary hypertension (renal, endocrine, or vascular disorders)
general_prevention: DASH diet (low sodium, rich in fruits and vegetables)
general_treatment: Lifestyle modification and physician-prescribed antihypertensive medications (e.g. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, CCBs)
warning_signs: Systolic BP > 180 mmHg or Diastolic > 120 mmHg with chest pain, vision changes, or shortness of breath (Hypertensive Crisis)
when_to_seek_doctor: Regular medical checks are essential; seek immediate emergency care for hypertensive crisis symptoms.

faqs.q: Why is hypertension called a silent killer?
faqs.a: Because it often has no obvious symptoms until it causes serious damage such as heart attack or stroke.

source: American Heart Association (AHA) / ACC Hypertension Guidelines

name: Gastritis
simple_definition: Inflammation, irritation, or erosion of the protective lining of the stomach.
medical_definition: Histologically confirmed inflammation of the gastric mucosa, which can be acute or chronic.
common_symptoms: Upper abdominal burning or gnawing pain
possible_causes: Regular use of NSAID pain relievers
general_treatment: Antacids, proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), H2 blockers, and antibiotic regimens for H. pylori as prescribed by a physician
when_to_seek_doctor: Consult a doctor if stomach pain persists over a week; seek immediate emergency care for gastrointestinal bleeding.

faqs.q: Can stress cause gastritis?
faqs.a: Severe physiological trauma or illness can cause acute stress gastritis, while mental stress can exacerbate gastric symptoms.

source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK)

name: GERD
simple_definition: A digestive disorder where stomach acid repeatedly flows back up into the food pipe (esophagus), causing heartburn.
medical_definition: Gastroesophageal reflux disease; a chronic digestive disease occurring when stomach acid or bile irritates the esophageal food pipe lining.
common_symptoms: Heartburn (burning sensation in chest after eating)
general_prevention: Elevating the head of the bed during sleep
Avoiding lying down within 3 hours of meals
general_treatment: Dietary modifications, physician-prescribed acid suppressants (PPIs, H2 receptor antagonists)
warning_signs: Persistent vomiting or choking sensation at night
when_to_seek_doctor: Consult a healthcare provider for frequent heartburn (more than twice a week) or difficulty swallowing.

faqs.q: Can GERD feel like a heart attack?
faqs.a: Yes, GERD chest discomfort can closely mimic cardiac pain; new or unexplained chest pain should always be medically evaluated immediately.

source: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Clinical Guidelines

name: UTI
simple_definition: An infection in any part of the urinary system, commonly affecting the bladder and urethra.
medical_definition: Urinary Tract Infection; an infection involving the kidneys, ureters, bladder, or urethra, most commonly caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli.
possible_causes: Bacterial colonization of the urinary tract (predominantly E. coli)
common_diagnostic_tests: Urinalysis (dipstick for nitrites and leukocyte esterase)
general_treatment: Appropriate course of doctor-prescribed targeted antibiotics and increased fluid intake
warning_signs: Flank or lower back pain (indicating possible kidney involvement / pyelonephritis)
when_to_seek_doctor: Medical evaluation is necessary to confirm infection and obtain appropriate antibiotic treatment.

faqs.q: Can a UTI go away without antibiotics?
faqs.a: While mild symptoms occasionally resolve, medical treatment is advised to prevent ascending infection to the kidneys.

source: CDC Urinary Tract Infection Overview

name: Tuberculosis
simple_definition: A serious bacterial infection mainly affecting the lungs, marked by chronic cough, night sweats, and weight loss.
medical_definition: A potentially fatal contagious airborne bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
possible_causes: Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmission through airborne droplets
risk_factors: Close contact with active TB cases
common_diagnostic_tests: Sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture
general_treatment: Directly Observed Therapy (DOTS) with a standardized multi-drug antibiotic regimen taken consistently for 6 months or longer under strict medical supervision
warning_signs: Massive hemoptysis (coughing large amounts of blood)
when_to_seek_doctor: Any cough lasting more than 2-3 weeks or coughing up blood requires prompt medical evaluation.

faqs.q: Is TB completely curable?
faqs.a: Yes, if the full course of prescribed anti-TB medications is taken strictly as directed without interruption.

source: World Health Organization (WHO) Global Tuberculosis Report

name: Anemia
simple_definition: A condition in which the blood lacks enough healthy red blood cells or hemoglobin to carry adequate oxygen to tissues.
medical_definition: A clinical state characterized by a quantitative deficiency in circulating hemoglobin concentration or red blood cell mass.
common_symptoms: Shortness of breath on mild exertion
general_prevention: Iron-rich diet (spinach, legumes, meat, fortified cereals)
Vitamin C to enhance iron absorption
common_diagnostic_tests: Complete Blood Count (CBC - Hemoglobin, RBC, Hematocrit)
general_treatment: Identification and treatment of the underlying cause, dietary enhancement, and physician-prescribed iron or vitamin supplementation
warning_signs: Extreme pallor accompanied by shortness of breath
when_to_seek_doctor: Medical evaluation is necessary to investigate the specific cause of anemia rather than self-treating with supplements.

faqs.q: Why is hemoglobin important?
faqs.a: Hemoglobin is the iron-containing protein in red blood cells that transports oxygen throughout the entire body.

source: World Health Organization (WHO) Anaemia Factsheet

name: Sinusitis
simple_definition: Inflammation or swelling of the tissue lining the sinuses around the forehead, cheeks, and eyes.
medical_definition: Rhinosinusitis; inflammation of the paranasal sinuses and nasal cavity mucosa, commonly secondary to viral or bacterial infection or allergy.
common_symptoms: Facial pressure or pain around eyes and cheeks
general_prevention: Avoiding cigarette smoke and environmental irritants
common_diagnostic_tests: Nasal endoscopy or CT scan if chronic or recurrent
general_treatment: Saline nasal irrigation, warm compresses, physician-recommended nasal steroid sprays or decongestants, antibiotics only if bacterial infection is confirmed
warning_signs: Swelling or redness around the eyes
when_to_seek_doctor: Consult a healthcare provider if symptoms last more than 10 days without improvement or worsen after initial recovery.

faqs.q: Are all sinus infections bacterial?
faqs.a: No, the vast majority begin as viral infections following a cold and resolve without antibiotics.

source: American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery (AAO-HNS)

name: Food poisoning
simple_definition: An illness caused by eating food or drinking water contaminated with harmful bacteria, viruses, or toxins.
medical_definition: Acute gastroenteritis resulting from the ingestion of food contaminated with infectious organisms (e.g. Salmonella, Campylobacter, Norovirus) or microbial toxins.
risk_factors: Consuming undercooked meat, unpasteurized milk, or improperly stored foods
general_prevention: Washing hands, cutting boards, and utensils after handling raw meat
common_diagnostic_tests: Stool culture or multiplex gastrointestinal pathogen PCR in severe cases
general_treatment: Aggressive oral rehydration solutions (ORS) to replace fluids and electrolytes, gradual light diet, and medical care if severe
warning_signs: Inability to keep liquids down for 24 hours
Signs of severe dehydration (dry mouth, sunken eyes, minimal urination)
when_to_seek_doctor: Prompt medical attention is required for severe dehydration, bloody diarrhea, or symptoms in infants and the elderly.

faqs.q: What is the most important treatment for food poisoning?
faqs.a: Fluid and electrolyte replacement (oral rehydration) to prevent dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea.

source: CDC Foodborne Illness Division

name: Viral fever
simple_definition: An elevated body temperature caused by any number of underlying viral infections, often accompanied by generalized body aches.
medical_definition: An acute, febrile systemic state mediated by endogenously released pyrogens responding to viral replication within the host.
possible_causes: Diverse seasonal respiratory, enteroviral, or systemic viruses
general_prevention: Avoiding crowded enclosed spaces during outbreaks
common_diagnostic_tests: Complete Blood Count (CBC) to assess white blood cell pattern
Specific viral antigen tests if indicated
general_treatment: Rest, abundant oral fluid intake, lukewarm sponging, and physician-advised antipyretic medication (e.g., paracetamol)
warning_signs: Appearance of unexplained rash or petechiae
Stiff neck, photophobia, or altered alertness
when_to_seek_doctor: Consult a physician if fever remains elevated beyond 72 hours, does not respond to medication, or warning signs appear.

faqs.q: Should antibiotics be taken for viral fever?
faqs.a: No, antibiotics have no efficacy against viruses and should only be taken when prescribed by a doctor for confirmed bacterial complications.

source: World Health Organization (WHO) Clinical Guidelines

name: Chickenpox
simple_definition: A highly contagious viral infection that causes an itchy, blister-like rash all over the body.
medical_definition: Varicella; an acute, highly contagious viral disease caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), characterized by crops of pruritic vesicular lesions.
common_symptoms: Itchy skin rash turning into fluid-filled blisters
possible_causes: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) airborne transmission or direct contact with blister fluid
general_prevention: Varicella vaccination (two doses provide strong protection)
Isolating infected individuals until all blisters have scabbed over
common_diagnostic_tests: VZV PCR from lesion fluid if confirmation is required
general_treatment: Supportive care: calamine lotion, cool baths, trimmed fingernails to prevent secondary skin infection, antipyretics (avoiding aspirin in children due to Reye's syndrome risk)
warning_signs: Secondary bacterial infection of blisters (red, hot, swollen skin)
when_to_seek_doctor: Contact a doctor for pregnant women, newborns, or individuals with weakened immunity, or if lesions appear infected.

faqs.q: Can someone get chickenpox more than once?
faqs.a: Most people develop lifelong immunity, though the virus remains dormant in nerve tissues and can reactivate years later as shingles (herpes zoster).

source: CDC Varicella (Chickenpox) Guidelines
